title: Abandoned PA Turnpike Tunnel, Breezewood, Pennsylvania
seoTitle: Charter Bus to the Abandoned PA Turnpike, Breezewood
excerpt: A charter bus to the Abandoned PA Turnpike near Breezewood: what the walk to the tunnels involves, where a coach can park, and what your group must bring.

heroImage.alt: The dark mouth of an abandoned turnpike tunnel with cracked pavement leading into it

extraImage.alt: Cracked highway pavement reclaimed by grass on the abandoned Pennsylvania Turnpike

body.text: Thirteen miles of interstate highway, complete with tunnels, simply left behind. When the Pennsylvania Turnpike was rerouted in 1968 the old alignment through Rays Hill and Sideling Hill was abandoned where it stood, and it has been quietly falling apart ever since. It is one of the strangest days out in the state, and a charter bus to the Abandoned PA Turnpike is the sensible way to reach a trailhead with almost no parking.

About 8.5 miles of cracked four-lane highway running between two long tunnels, now known to cyclists as the Pike 2 Bike trail. Sideling Hill Tunnel runs roughly 6,800 feet and Rays Hill about 3,500. Both are completely unlit. Trees are pushing through the pavement, the lane markings are still faintly visible, and the whole thing has the specific atmosphere of infrastructure that outlived its purpose.

It draws a particular kind of group: history and engineering enthusiasts, photographers, urban explorers, cycling clubs and hiking groups. It is not a conventional sightseeing stop and it rewards people who find that interesting rather than people expecting an attraction.
The three things your group must bring

items: A real flashlight or headlamp per person. Phone flashlights are not adequate for a mile of unlit tunnel, and the middle of Sideling Hill is genuinely, completely dark.
Proper footwear. The surface is broken asphalt with standing water, loose gravel and debris. It is flat, but it is not smooth.
Layers. The tunnels stay cold year-round and are markedly colder than the trail outside, even in August.
Water and everything else you need. There are no facilities of any kind at either end — no restrooms, no water, no shelter.

body.text: Which charter bus suits the trip
The access roads to the trailheads are narrow rural lanes and the parking areas are small gravel lots that were never designed for coaches. This is the constraint that shapes the whole booking.

items: Twenty to thirty-two: a [mini bus](/fleet/mini-buses) is the right vehicle here. It reaches the trailheads, turns around at the end, and does not commit you to a drop-and-return arrangement.

Forty to fifty-six: a full-size [charter bus](/fleet/motor-coaches) is comfortable for the drive from Pittsburgh or Harrisburg, but confirm the specific trailhead and turning space before booking — plan on a drop-off with the coach waiting in Breezewood rather than at the trail.
Ten to fourteen: a [sprinter van](/fleet/sprinter-vans) suits a photography group working around the light at either tunnel mouth.

body.text: The on-board restroom matters more than usual on this trip, precisely because the destination has none.
Getting there and how long to allow

The site sits just off Interstate 70/76 near Breezewood, which puts it roughly two hours from Pittsburgh and about two and a half from Harrisburg. We run pickups from [Bedford](/locations/pennsylvania/bedford), [Somerset](/locations/pennsylvania/somerset), [Johnstown](/locations/pennsylvania/johnstown) and [Altoona](/locations/pennsylvania/altoona), all within an hour.

Allow four hours on the trail if you want to walk both tunnels and return, or two if you are only doing Sideling Hill from the northern end. Groups searching for charter bus rental near me for this trip should say clearly that the destination is an unmarked trailhead rather than a visitor attraction — the parking constraint is the whole logistical question, and an operator who has not asked about it has not thought about it.
Walking it, and what the tunnels are like inside

The grade is gentle — this was built for trucks — so the walking itself is undemanding. What is demanding is the dark. Sideling Hill takes about twenty minutes to walk end to end, and for a good portion of that you cannot see either portal. Groups consistently describe the middle section as the most disorienting few minutes of the day, and it is worth warning anybody who is uneasy in enclosed spaces before they commit to it.

Water drips constantly from the ceiling, the floor is puddled in places, and the acoustics are extraordinary — a group talking normally at one end is audible far further than anyone expects. Sound carries so well that it is worth agreeing in advance that people will keep together rather than spreading out along a mile of unlit tunnel.

The ventilation buildings above each portal are derelict and fenced. They are interesting to photograph from the trail and should not be entered; the structures have been unmaintained for over fifty years.

items: May to October: the most reliable footing and the longest daylight. The best window for a group.
October: autumn color along the approach, and the most photogenic time of year on the open sections.
Winter: the tunnels can hold ice and the access roads are not a priority for plowing. Workable for a small, well-equipped group and not advisable for a large one.
